Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verses 1–2:

Ka'b said: The beginning of al-An'am is the beginning of the Torah. ﴿And He made the darknesses and the light﴾. Here "made" (ja'ala) means "created." The "darknesses" are the night, and the "light" is the day, along with the radiance that is in the sun, the moon, and other things. The word "light" is singular because it is intended as a category (jins). In this verse there is a refutation of the Magians (al-Majus) in their worship of fire and other lights, and in their claim that good comes from light and evil from darkness, for a created thing cannot be a god or the agent of any event. ﴿Yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾. "Ya'dilun" means they make equals and likenesses, from your saying: "I equated (adaltu) so-and-so with so-and-so," when you make him its counterpart and peer. "Thumma" (yet/then) is used here to indicate the improbability that they would ascribe equals to their Lord after the clarity of His signs in creating the heavens and the earth, and the darknesses and the light. Likewise His saying: ﴿Yet you doubt﴾ indicates the improbability that they would doubt in this after it has been established that He gives them life and causes them to die. Within this is an expression of wonder at their action and a rebuke of them. ﴿Those who disbelieve﴾ here is general, covering every polytheist. It may also be specific to the Magians, by the evidence of "the darknesses and the light," and to the worshippers of idols, because they were the neighbours of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the refutation in most of the Qur'an falls upon them. ﴿He created you from clay﴾: that is, He created your father Adam from clay. ﴿Then He decreed a term, and a named term is with Him﴾. The first term is death, and the second is the Day of Resurrection. His placing it "with Him" is because He alone has knowledge of it. It was also said: the first term is sleep and the second is death. "Thumma" is used here to order the reports, not to order the occurrence, because the decree precedes the creation.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 3:

﴿He is Allah, in the heavens and on the earth.﴾ "In the heavens" (fi al-samawat) is connected to the meaning of the Name of Allah. So the sense is like His saying: ﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven, and God on the earth﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 84], just as one says: "The Commander of the Believers, the Caliph, is in the East and the West." It is also possible that the prepositional phrase is in the position of the predicate, so that it is connected to an omitted active participle (ism fa'il); the meaning on this reading is close to the first. It has also been said: the meaning is that He is in the heavens and the earth through His knowledge, like His saying: ﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾ [al-Hadid: 4]. The first is more preferred and more eloquent, because the Name Allah comprises all the attributes: knowledge, power, wisdom, and others, so it gathers them all with brevity. The second is strengthened by the fact that the context of the speech concerns Allah's being aware and His knowledge, based on His saying after it: ﴿He knows your secret and your open declaration﴾. It has also been said: it is connected to an omitted element whose estimated meaning is: "the one worshipped in the heavens and in the earth," and this omitted element is a description of Allah; the Name Allah, on this view, and on the first view, is the predicate of the subject. As for when the prepositional phrase is the predicate, then "Allah" is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 6, verses 4–5:**

﴿And no sign from the signs of their Lord comes to them﴾. The first *min* (مِنْ) here is extra (*zā'idah*, grammatically superfluous). The second is partitive (*lil-tab'īḍ*, indicating a part of the whole) or specifying the kind (*li-bayān al-jins*, clarifying the category). ﴿with the truth﴾, meaning what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. ﴿So they will soon receive﴾ the news. This is a warning of punishment and retribution for their mockery.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 6:

﴿Did they not see how many generations We destroyed before them, whom We had established on the earth as We have not established you?﴾ This is an exhortation to the disbelievers to take heed from others before them. The qarn (generation) is a hundred years; it is also said seventy, and it is also said forty. ﴿We established them on the earth﴾: the pronoun refers to qarn, because it carries the meaning of a group. ﴿As We have not established for you﴾: the address is to all the people of that age, both believers and disbelievers. ﴿And We sent down the sky upon them in abundant rain﴾: "sky" here means the rain and the clouds, or it may be the sky in its literal sense; and midraran (abundant) is an intensive form of intensification, from your saying darra al-matar (the rain poured forth) when it was plentiful. ﴿So We destroyed them for their sins﴾: the implied meaning is: they disbelieved and disobeyed, so We destroyed them. This is a warning to the disbelievers that there may befall them the like of what befell those people, despite their strength and their establishment.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 7:

﴿And even if We had sent down to you a written scripture on paper⁠⁠﴾ etc.: This is an informing that they will not believe even if the clearest signs came to them. The meaning of His words ﴿and they touched it with their hands⁠⁠﴾ is that even if they had gone to the extreme of examining it and turning it over so that doubt would be removed, they would have persisted in obstinacy. It is likely that the cause of this verse was the statement of some of them to the Prophet (ﷺ): "I will not believe in you until you bring a book from the heavens ordering me to believe you," and "I do not think that, even with this, I would believe you."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 8–10:

﴿And they say: "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?"﴾ This is a report of the demand of some of the Arabs. It is narrated that al-'Āṣ ibn Wā'il, al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad and al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghūth said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Muhammad, if only there were an angel with you." ﴿Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided.﴾ Ibn 'Abbās said: The meaning is: had We sent down an angel and they then disbelieved, the punishment would have been hastened upon them. In the speech there is, on this reading, an ellipsis, and "the matter was decided" means: the hastening of their seizure. It was also said: the meaning is that had We sent down an angel, they would have died from the terror of seeing him, and "the matter was decided" on this reading means: their death. ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man.﴾ That is, had We made the Messenger an angel, he would have appeared in the form of a man, because they have no capacity to see an angel in his own form. ﴿And We would have confused them with what they confuse.﴾ That is, We would have obscured for them what they obscure for themselves and for their weak followers, for if they saw the angel in the form of a human, they would say: "This is a human and not an angel." ﴿And messengers before you were certainly mocked﴾ — the verse is a report intended to console the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding what he suffered from his people. ﴿So there descended upon those who mocked them that which they used to mock﴾ — that is, it encompassed them. In this report there is a warning to the disbelievers.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 11:

﴿Say: Travel through the earth⦆ — the verse; he urges reflection (i'tibar) upon others when they see the dwellings of the disbelievers who perished before them. ﴿Then observe⦆ — al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the difference between His saying "fa-unzuru" (so observe) and His saying "thumma unzuru" (then observe)? I say: He made observing a consequence of traveling in His saying "fa-unzuru," as if He said: travel in order to observe. As for His saying "fa-siru fi al-ard thumma unzuru" (so travel through the earth, then observe), its meaning is the permissibility of travel for trade and other benefits, and the obligation of observing those who perished; He arranged it upon that with "thumma" (then), because of the great distance between the obligatory and the permissible.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 12:

﴿Say, "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?" Say, "To Allah."﴾ The purpose of the verse is to establish proof for the soundness of tawhid (monotheism) and the refutation of shirk (associating partners with God). This is conveyed in the form of a question in order to establish the argument against the disbelievers. He first asked, "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?" Then he answered the question with His words, "Say, 'To Allah.'" This is because the disbelievers necessarily agree to this. Thereby it is established that the true God is Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth. It is only fitting for the questioner to answer his own question when he knows that his opponent will not contradict him in the answer by which he establishes the proof against him. ﴿He has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ meaning, He has decreed it. The explanation of this is the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, Allah wrote a book before He created the heavens and the earth, and in it: 'My mercy precedes My wrath,'" and in another narration: "overcomes My wrath." ﴿He will surely gather you﴾ is detached from what precedes it, and it is the answer to an implied oath. It was also said that it is an explanation of the mercy mentioned, with the meaning: "that He gather you." This is weak, because the heavy nun (نّ) enters in a place where it does not belong, as it only enters with an oath or in non-obligatory contexts. ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾ It was said: here "ilā" (إلى) means "fī" (في), which is weak; the correct view is that it indicates the endpoint in its usual sense. ﴿Those who have lost themselves, they will not believe﴾ "Those" (الذين) is the subject, and its predicate is "they will not believe." The fa' (فـ) entered because the sentence contains the meaning of a condition; this was said by al-Zajjaj and it is good. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Those" is in the accusative to express blame, or in the nominative as the predicate of an implied subject. It was also said that it is a substitute for the pronoun in "la-yajmaannakum," which is weak; and it was said that it is a vocative, which is invalid.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 13–14:

﴿And to Him belongs whatever dwells in the night and the day.﴾ It is coordinated with His saying "Say: To Allah," and "sakana" means "resided," so it is from "sukna" (dwelling). It was also said that it is from "sukun" (stillness), but this is weak, because things are both still and moving, so the word would not be general. The intended meaning is the generality of His dominion over everything. ﴿Say: Shall I take other than Allah as a protector?﴾ This is an establishment of proof against the disbelievers, and a rebuttal to them through the attributes of the Generous Allah, in which none shares with Him. ﴿The first to submit⦆ meaning: of this community, because the Prophet (ﷺ) is the forerunner of his community to Islam. ﴿And never be among⦆ there is an ellipsis in the speech; its estimate is "and it was said to me: 'And never be among the polytheists'," or it is coordinated with the meaning of "I was commanded," so there is no ellipsis, and its estimate is "I was commanded to submit to Islam and forbidden to associate partners."

﴿Whoever is turned away from it on that Day, Allah has indeed shown him mercy.﴾ That is, whoever is turned away from the punishment on the Day of Resurrection, Allah has indeed shown him mercy. It is also recited as "yuṣraf" with the yā' vowelled with a fatḥa, and its subject is Allah. ﴿And that﴾ refers either to the turning away of the punishment or to the mercy.

And if Allah should touch you with harm, there is none to remove it except Him. Its meaning: "yamsaska" means "yusibaka" (afflicts you). "Ḍurr" (harm) means illness and other things, in general, covering all harmful things; and "khayr" (good) means well-being and other things, also in general. The verse is a proof of Divine Oneness, since Allah the Exalted alone holds sole power over harm and good. Likewise, the attributes that follow it are proofs and a refutation of the polytheists.

﴿Say: "What thing is greatest as a witness?"﴾ This is a question that calls for an answer on which the intended meaning is built. It is evidence that "thing" may be said of God, yet ﴿there is nothing like unto Him﴾.

﴿Say: "God is witness between me and you."﴾ This admits of two readings. The first is that Allah is the mubtada' (subject of the nominal sentence) and "witness" (shahid) is its khabar (predicate). The second is that the answer is complete at His words, "Say: 'Allah'", meaning that Allah is the greatest witness, and then a new sentence begins, with the sense "He is witness between me and you." The first reading is stronger because it involves no implied pronoun (idmar), and the second is stronger because it matches the question. The question is like someone asking, "Who is the greatest of people?" and the answer being given, "So-and-so," with the implied meaning "So-and-so is the greatest."

The purpose of the statement is to call upon God as a witness to the truthfulness of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). God's witnessing to this is His knowledge of the soundness of the prophethood of our master Muhammad (ﷺ) and His manifesting of his miracle, which indicates his prophethood.

﴿and whoever it reaches﴾ is conjoined to the object pronoun in ﴿that I may warn you﴾. The subject of "reaches" is the pronoun referring to the Qur'an, and the object is omitted, referring to "whoever", with the sense "and whoever it reaches." The meaning is: this Qur'an was revealed to me so that I may warn with it those addressed, who are the people of Makkah, and warn everyone the Qur'an reaches, from among the Arabs and non-Arabs, until the Day of Resurrection. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Whoever the Qur'an reaches, it is as if he has seen the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." It was also said that the meaning is: "and whoever reaches puberty," though this is far-fetched.

﴿Are you indeed bearing witness that there are other gods with God?﴾ This is a confrontation of the polytheists with their polytheism. Then He disavowed that by saying, "I do not bear witness," and then God bore witness to His oneness. It is narrated that it was revealed concerning a group of disbelievers who came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "O Muhammad, do you know of any other god with Allah?"

They recognise him as they recognise their own sons. [Tashil cross-reference: see al-Baqarah, 146.] ﴿Those who have ruined themselves—they do not believe.﴾ "Those who" (alladhina) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "they do not believe." It was also said that "those who" is an attributive modifier (na't) of "those to whom We gave the Book," but this is unsound, because those who were given the Book were not cited here except to establish the proof against the disbelievers.

﴿And who is more unjust﴾: its wording is interrogative, but its meaning is "no one is more unjust"—﴿than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾. This is a disavowal of lying about Allah and a demonstration of the innocence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from what they attributed to him of falsehood. It is also possible that by "fabricating against Allah" he means what the disbelievers attributed to Him of partners and offspring. ﴿Or denies His signs﴾, i.e., His signs and proofs. ﴿Where are your partners﴾: this is said to them as a rebuke. ﴿whom you claimed﴾, i.e., you claimed that they are gods; the object was omitted because the meaning indicates it. The governing element of "the Day We will gather them" is omitted.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 23:

﴿Then their trial will be nothing﴾ Al-fitna (trial, test; here, the outcome of disbelief) here may mean disbelief, that is, the outcome of their disbelief will be nothing but their denial of it and their disavowal of it. It was also said: their fitna is their excuse; and it was said: their speech. It is recited fitnatuhum with the accusative, making the predicate of kana (was) and its subject ﴿an qalu﴾ (that they said); and it is recited with the nominative, making kana's subject and predicate ﴿an qalu﴾ (that they said). ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ is a denial of their polytheism. If it is asked: how can they deny it when Allah has said: ﴿and they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ (4:42)? The answer is that this differs according to the varieties of people and the varying situations: some people conceal and others acknowledge, and they conceal in one situation and acknowledge in another, because the Day of Resurrection is long. Ibn Abbas, when asked about this question, said: They denied it out of hope for salvation, so Allah sealed their mouths, and their limbs spoke, so they will not conceal from Allah any statement.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 25:

﴿And among them are those who listen to you.﴾ The pronoun refers back to the disbelievers. He used the singular "yastami'" (listens) although it is a verb of a plural subject, taking the wording of "man" (whoever) into account.

﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it.﴾ "Akinnah" is the plural of "kinan," which means a covering. "An yafqahuhu" (lest they understand it) is in the position of an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih, object of purpose), and its implied sense is: "out of aversion to their understanding it." The meaning of the verse is that God places a barrier between them and understanding the Qur'an when they listen to it. The imagery of coverings and deafness is used for emphasis (mubalaghah), and it is a metaphor (isti'arah).

﴿Tales of the ancients.﴾ That is, their stories and reports. It is the plural of "asfar" and "usturah" (a tale, legend). Al-Suhayli said: Wherever "tales of the ancients" occurs in the Qur'an, the one who said it is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. He had entered the land of Persia and learned the reports of its kings, and so he would say: "My narration is better than the narration of Muhammad ﷺ."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 26:

﴿And they forbid others from it, and keep away from it themselves.﴾ The pronoun "they" (hum) refers to the disbelievers, and the pronoun in "from it" (anhu) refers to the Qur'an. The meaning is: they forbid people from faith, while they themselves keep away from it, that is, they distance themselves. Al-na'y (distancing) is al-bu'd (distance). It has also been said that the pronoun in "from it" refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). The meaning of "they forbid from it" is that they forbid people from harming him, while they themselves keep away from him. According to this view, the verse refers to Abu Talib and those who were with him: he protected the Prophet (ﷺ) but did not submit (to Islam). In his saying "yanhawna" and "yan'awna" there is a kind of tajnis (paronomasia).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 33:

﴿Indeed, We know that what they say grieves you﴾ Nafi' recited "yahzunu" wherever it occurs with a damma on the yaa', from ahzana (to grieve), except in His saying: ﴿The great terror will not grieve them﴾. The rest of the reciters read it with a fatha on the yaa', from the triliteral hazina, and this is more well-known in the language. "What they say" refers to their saying that he is a sorcerer, a poet, and a soothsayer. ﴿So it is not you they deny﴾. As for the one who recited with the shaddah (tashdid), the meaning is: they do not deny you while believing you to be a liar; rather, they reject the truth while knowing it. As for the one who recited with the lightening (takhfif), it has been said that its meaning is: they do not find you to be a liar. It is said: akdhabtu fulanan (I found so-and-so to be a liar) when you find him to be a liar, just as it is said: ahmadtuhu (I found him praiseworthy) when you find him praiseworthy. It has also been said that it has the same meaning as the shaddah: kadhdhabaka fulan and akdhabahu fulan both mean the same thing. This is the most apparent view, because of His saying afterwards: "they deny" (yajhadun). This is supported by what is reported: that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl, for he said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "We do not disbelieve in you, but we deny what you have brought." And he said to al-Akhnas ibn Shariq: "By Allah, Muhammad is truthful, but I envy him for his nobility." ﴿But it is the wrongdoers﴾: that is, but they (are the ones who deny), and the apparent noun (al-zahir) was placed in the position of the pronoun (al-mudmar) to indicate that they wronged themselves in their denial.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 34:

﴿And indeed, messengers were denied before you﴾, etc. This is a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), an urging upon him to be patient, and a promise to him of victory. ﴿And none can alter the words of Allah﴾, that is, His promises to His messengers, as in His saying: ﴿And Our word had already preceded to Our servants, the messengers, that they would surely be given victory﴾ [al-Saffat: 172]. In this there is a reinforcement of the promise. ﴿And there has certainly come to you some of the news of the messengers﴾, that is, some of their reports, meaning by that their patience and then their victory. This also serves as a reinforcement of the promise and an urging to patience. The subject of jaa'aka (ﷺ) [the verb "came to you"] is elided; its estimated form is "naba'" (news) or "khabar" (report). It was said that the subject is the prepositional phrase (al-majrur) itself.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 35:

﴿And if their turning away has been hard for you﴾ etc.: its purpose is to urge the Prophet (ﷺ) toward patience and submission to what God wills for His servants, whether faith or disbelief, for he (ﷺ) was intensely eager for their faith. So it was said to him: "If you are able to go down into the earth (nafaq) or ascend into the sky and bring them a sign by which they would believe, then do so, but you are not able to do that." So submit to the command of God. The nafaq in the earth means an opening through which one passes into what is beneath the earth. The answer to "in" (in) has been omitted because the meaning is understood. ﴿And had God willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾: this is an argument for the People of the Sunnah against the Qadariyya. ﴿So do not be among the ignorant﴾: i.e., among those who are ignorant that God, had He willed, would have gathered them upon guidance.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 36:

﴿Only those who listen will respond﴾. The meaning: only those who listen, and so understand and reflect, will respond to you. ﴿As for the dead, Allah will raise them up﴾. In this there are three interpretations. The first: the dead refers metaphorically to the disbelievers, whose hearts are dead, and "raising" (al-ba'th) refers to their gathering on the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is that the disbelievers in this world are like the dead in their poor hearing and lack of understanding, so Allah will raise them in the Hereafter, and then they will hear. The second: the dead refers to the disbelievers, and "raising" refers to their being guided to understanding and hearing. The third: the dead is to be taken literally, and the raising is to be taken literally, so it is a report about the raising of the dead on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 37:

﴿And they say: "Why has a sign not been sent down upon him from his Lord?"﴾ The pronoun in "qalu" (they said) refers to the disbelievers, and "lawla" (why not) here expresses a demand. The meaning is that they asked the Prophet ﷺ to bring a sign as proof of his prophethood. If it is said: he had already brought signs, and his miracles were many, so why did they ask for a sign? The answer is in two respects. First, they did not consider what he had brought to be significant, and it was as though he had brought nothing at all in their view, because of their obstinacy and denial. Second, they only wanted a sign that would compel them to faith without reflection or contemplation.

﴿Say: "Indeed, Allah is able to send down a sign"﴾ is a reply to their statement. This saying of theirs is related in several places in the Qur'an, and it was answered with various responses. Among them is a response that rebukes them for their demand for signs, since He had indeed brought them signs, and seeking what is already attained (tahsil al-hasil) is not fitting, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made the signs clear﴾ [al-Baqarah: 118], and His saying: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book, which is recited to them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 51]. Among them is a response that calls for turning away from them, because when the opponent's obstinacy is evident, debating with him is dropped. His saying ﴿Say: "Indeed, Allah is able to send down a sign"﴾ may be of this kind. It may also mean that He is able to send down a sign that compels them to faith.

﴿But most of them do not know﴾. The object of "yalamun" (they know) is omitted, and it may have two meanings. The first: they do not know that Allah is able. The second: they do not know that Allah has withheld the signs that would compel them to faith for the sake of the welfare of His servants, for if they saw them and still did not believe, they would be punished with the chastisement.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 38:

﴿بِجَنَاحَيْهِ﴾ is an emphasis, clarification and removal of the metaphor commonly associated with this word, for it is said: "a bird" (ṭāʾir) of good fortune and ill fortune. ﴿أُمَمٌ أَمْثَالُكُمْ﴾ means: they are like you in creation and provision, in life and death, and in other respects. The connection of this statement to what precedes it is in two respects. The first is that it is an admonition concerning the creatures of God Most High, as if He were saying: reflect upon His creatures, and do not seek other signs beyond them. The second is an admonition concerning the Resurrection, as if He were saying: all beasts and birds will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection just as you will be gathered, and this is more apparent in view of His words that follow: ﴿ثُمَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّهِمْ يُحْشَرُونَ﴾ ("Then to their Lord they will be gathered"). ﴿مَّا فَرَّطْنَا فِي ٱلكِتَٰبِ مِن شَيْءٍ﴾ means: We have not neglected anything. "The Book" here is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), and the statement according to this view is general. It was also said that it refers to the Qur'an, and according to this view the statement is specific: that is, We have not neglected in it anything that contains your guidance and clarification for you. ﴿ثُمَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّهِمْ يُحْشَرُونَ﴾ means: the beasts and birds will be raised on the Day of Resurrection for recompense and for judgment among them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 39–41:

﴿And those who denied Our signs are deaf and dumb⦘ — the verse: When He mentioned His power to resurrect all of creation, He followed it by describing those who denied this as deaf and dumb, and His saying "in darknesses" takes the place of describing them as blind. ﴿Say: Tell me⦘ means "inform me," and the second pronoun is for address, having no place in i'rab (grammatical case). The answer to the conditional is omitted, and its estimated form is: "If the punishment of Allah comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, whom will you call upon?" Then He made them acknowledge that they would not call upon anyone at that time except Allah, and would not call upon their gods. The verse is an argument against them, an affirmation of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), and a refutation of shirk (associating partners with God). ﴿If He wills⦘ is an exception, meaning: He removes what has descended upon you if He wills, and afflicts you with it if He wills. ﴿And you forget what you associate⦘ may be from forgetting (nisyan) or from abandoning (tark).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 52:

﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾ etc. It was revealed concerning the weak among the believers, such as Bilal, 'Ammar ibn Yasir, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, Khabbab, Suhayb, and those like them. Some of the polytheists of Quraysh had said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We cannot mix with these people because of our nobility; so if you drive them away, we will follow you." So this verse was revealed. ﴿In the morning and the evening﴾: it is said that this refers to the prayer in Makkah before the five daily prayers were made obligatory, when they were performed at morning and evening. It is also said that it is an expression for the continuity of the act. "Call upon" here means to invoke and remember God, or it means worship. ﴿Desiring His Face﴾: a report about their sincerity towards God, and in it is a praise of them. ﴿Nothing of their account is upon you at all﴾ etc. It is said: the pronoun in "their account" refers to those who call upon their Lord; and it is said: it refers to the polytheists, and the meaning on this view is: you are not responsible for them, and they are not responsible for you, so do not concern yourself with their affairs to the point of driving these away on their account. The first view is more likely, due to His saying: ﴿And I am not one to drive away those who believe﴾ [Hud: 29], and His saying: ﴿Their account is only upon my Lord﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 113]. The meaning on this view is that God is the one who calls them to account, so for what reason would you drive them away? ﴿So that you would drive them away﴾: this is the answer to the negation in His saying "nothing of their account is upon you." ﴿And then you would be among the wrongdoers﴾: this is the answer to the prohibition in His saying "and do not drive away," or it is coordinated with "so that you would drive them away."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 53–54:

﴿And thus We have tried some of them by means of others﴾ meaning: We tested the disbelievers by means of the believers. That was because the disbelievers used to say: "Are these the slaves and the poor, whom God has favoured with guidance to the truth and with happiness rather than us, when we are the nobles and the wealthy?" They said this in a tone of disbelief and disdain. ﴿Is not God most knowing of those who give thanks?﴾ This is a refutation of the disbelievers in their earlier statement. ﴿And when those who believe in Our signs come to you, say: "Peace be upon you."﴾ They are the ones whom the Prophet (ﷺ) was forbidden to drive away; rather, he was commanded to greet them with peace, to honour them, and to put them at ease with what follows. ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ meaning: He has made it binding upon Himself. In the Sahih it is related: "Indeed God wrote a book, and it is with Him above the Throne: 'Indeed My mercy precedes My wrath.'" ﴿That whoever of you does evil in ignorance﴾ up to the end of the verse: it promises forgiveness and mercy to whoever repents and makes amends. It is addressed to the people mentioned earlier, and its ruling is general to them and to others. The meaning of ignorance (jahalah) has been mentioned in Surah al-Nisa' [16]. It is also said: it was revealed because 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (رضي الله عنه) advised the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to drive away the weak, in the hope that the disbelievers would embrace Islam. When the verse "Do not drive them away" was revealed, 'Umar regretted his words and repented of them, and then this verse was revealed. It has been read as ﴿annahu﴾ with a fatha, as a substitute for "mercy," and with a kasra, as a new sentence. Likewise ﴿fa-annahu ghafurun rahim﴾ is read with a kasra as a new sentence, and with a fatha as the predicate of an implied subject, its sense being: "So his command is that He is Forgiving and Merciful." It is also said: it is a repetition of the first, because of the length of the speech.

﴿Say: "If I had what you are asking to hasten, the matter would already have been decided."﴾ That is: if the punishment were with me according to the first interpretation, and the proposed signs according to the other interpretation, the separation would have taken place and the dispute would have ended, either by the descent of the punishment or by the appearance of the signs.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 59:

﴿Mafatih al-ghayb (the keys of the unseen)﴾ is a metaphor, an expression for reaching the unseen, just as one reaches what is in the treasuries by means of keys. It is the plural of miftah (with a kasra on the mim), meaning "key." It may also be the plural of mafth (with a fatha on the mim), meaning "treasury." ﴿Nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth﴾ is a reminder, through it, of other things, because it is more hidden than anything else. ﴿In a clear record﴾ is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). It was also said: it is the knowledge of God.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashīl) on Surah 6, verse 60:

﴿It is He who takes you back [in sleep] at night﴾, i.e., when you sleep. In this there is a lesson and an argument for the resurrection in the Hereafter. ﴿What you have earned﴾, i.e., the deeds you have done. ﴿Then He raises you up therein﴾, i.e., He wakes you from sleep. The pronoun refers to the day, because waking mostly occurs in it, and sleeping mostly occurs at night. ﴿A term appointed﴾, i.e., the appointed term of death.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verses 61–66:

﴿Ḥafaẓah﴾ (guardians), the plural of ḥāfiẓ (guardian), and they are the recording angels. ﴿Tawaffat-hu rusulunā﴾ (our messengers take him in death): i.e., the angels who are with the Angel of Death. ﴿Thumma ruddū﴾ (then they are returned): a shift from direct address to the third person, and the pronoun refers to all of creation. ﴿Qul man yunajjīkum﴾ (Say: "Who delivers you?") to the end of the verse: this is the establishment of proof. "The darknesses of the land and the sea" is an expression for their hardships and terrors, just as a difficult day is called "dark." ﴿ʿAdhāban min fawqikum aw min taḥti arjulikum﴾ (a punishment from above you or from beneath your feet). It has been said: what comes from above is the raining down of stones, and from beneath is the earthquake (khasf). It has also been said: "from above you" is the domination of your elders, and "from beneath your feet" is the domination of your lowly ones; but this is far-fetched. ﴿Aw yalbisakum shiyaʿan﴾ (or confuse you into factions), i.e., mix you into divided, opposing groups. ﴿Wa yudhīqa baʿḍakum baʾsa baʿḍ﴾ (and make some of you taste the violence of others): through fighting. Scholars differed over whether this verse is addressed to the disbelievers or to the believers. It is narrated that when the verse ﴿an yabʿatha ʿalaykum ʿadhāban min fawqikum﴾ (that He may send upon you a punishment from above you) was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I seek refuge in Your Face." When ﴿min taḥti arjulikum﴾ (from beneath your feet) was revealed, he said: "I seek refuge in Your Face." When ﴿aw yalbisakum shiyaʿan﴾ (or confuse you into factions) was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This is easier." So Allah decreed for this Ummah strife and fighting until the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Wa kadhdhaba bihi qawmuka﴾ (Yet your people denied it): the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, or to the preceding threat, and "your people" are the Quraysh. ﴿Lastu ʿalaykum bi-wakīl﴾ (I am not a guardian over you): i.e., not a keeper or one who compels you. In this there is [a verse] of abandonment (mutarakah), whose ruling was abrogated by the verse of fighting.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 67:

﴿For every news there is a fixed time (mustaqarr)﴾ — that is, a limit at which one will know who was truthful and who was lying. ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses﴾ — in mockery of them and disparagement of them. ﴿Then turn away from them﴾ — that is, stand up and do not sit with them. ﴿And if Satan should cause you to forget﴾ — "in" (إما) is compounded of the conditional particle "in" (إن) and the superfluous "ma" (ما), and the meaning is: if Satan causes you to forget the prohibition against sitting with them, then do not sit after you have remembered the prohibition.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verses 68–69:

﴿And there is nothing upon those who fear Allah for their account at all﴾. Those who fear (yattaqun) are the believers. The pronoun in "their account" (hisabihim) refers to the disbelievers and the mockers. The meaning is: the believers bear nothing of the account of the disbelievers for their mockery and their leading others astray. It was said that this implies the permissibility of the believers sitting with the disbelievers, since the prohibition of that was burdensome to them, given that they must necessarily mix with them in seeking a livelihood, in circumambulating the House, and in other matters. Then it was abrogated (nusikha) by the verse in al-Nisa', which is ﴿And He has already sent down to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 140], and so on. It was also said that it does not imply the permissibility of sitting (with them) at all.

﴿But it is a reminder, that perhaps they may fear Allah﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first is that the meaning is: there is no accountability of the disbelievers upon the believers, but upon them (the believers) is a reminder to them (the disbelievers) and admonition. The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of "reminder" (dhikra) on this view is either accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), its implied sense being "they remind them with a reminder," or nominative as the subject, its implied sense being "upon them is a reminder." The pronoun in "perhaps they" (la'allahum) refers to the disbelievers, i.e., they remind them in hope that they will fear Allah; or it refers to the believers, i.e., they remind them so that their reminder and admonition become fear of Allah. The second interpretation: the meaning is that the prohibition of the believers from sitting with the disbelievers is not due to the fact that there is some of their account upon them; rather, it is a reminder for the believers. The i'rab of "reminder" on this view is either the predicate of an omitted subject, its implied sense being: "but their prohibition is a reminder," or an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih), its implied sense being: "they were only forbidden as a reminder." On this view, the pronoun in "perhaps they" refers to the believers only.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 70:

﴿And leave those who﴾ It is said that it is an abandonment (mutarakah) abrogated by the sword (naskh bi-l-sayf); and it is said: rather, it is a threat, so there is neither abandonment nor abrogation in it. ﴿have taken their religion as amusement and diversion﴾ That is, they have taken the religion that was incumbent upon them as amusement and diversion, because they mocked us, and they took the religion they believe in as amusement and diversion; because they do not believe in the Resurrection, so they play and divert themselves. ﴿And remind by it﴾ The pronoun refers to the religion or to the Qur'an. ﴿lest a soul be delivered to ruin (tubsala)﴾ It is said: its meaning is "lest it be detained"; it is said: "lest it be disgraced"; it is said: "lest it be destroyed." Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 71:

﴿Say, "Shall we call upon, instead of Allah, that which can neither benefit us nor harm us, and be turned back on our heels after Allah has guided us, like one whom the devils have enticed away into bewilderment, while he has companions who call him to guidance, saying, 'Come to us'?"﴾ The verse: it is an establishment of proof and a rebuke to the disbelievers. ﴿And be turned back on our heels﴾: that is, return from guidance to misguidance. This is a clause conjoined to "shall we call upon", and the hamzah in it is for denunciation and rebuke. ﴿Like one whom the devils have enticed away﴾: the kaf (ka, "like") is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "nuruddu" (we be turned back): that is, how could we return resembling one whom the devils have enticed; or it is an adjective to an omitted verbal noun, its estimated form being "a return like the return of the one who...". The meaning of "istahwathu al-shayāṭīn" (the devils have enticed him): they carried him off into the wastelands and led him away from the road. It is from hawā, yahwī (to fall/descend), when one goes down into the earth; and al-Fārisī said: istahwā means ahwā (to cause to fall), like istadhalla means adhalla (to humiliate). ﴿Bewildered﴾: that is, lost from the road; it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from the object in "istahwathu". ﴿He has companions who call him to guidance, "Come to us"﴾: that is, this one who has been enticed has companions, who are a group calling him to guidance, meaning to guide him to the road, saying to him, "Come to us"; but he has wandered and gone far from them, so he does not answer them. It was also said: it was revealed concerning ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, when his father was calling him to Islam. This view is refuted by the statement of ʿĀ'isha: "Nothing of the Qur'an was revealed concerning the family of Abū Bakr except my innocence."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verses 72–73:

﴿And that you establish prayer﴾ is conjoined (ʿatf) to "li-nuslima" (that we may submit), or to the object of "umirna" (we were commanded). ﴿His word is the truth﴾ is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "yawma yaqulu" (on the day He says), which is placed before it. The governing element (al-ʿamil) in it is the sense of settledness (al-istiqrar), as in your saying "yawm al-jumʿa al-qital" (the fighting is on Friday). "Al-yawm" here means "al-hin" (a time), and the agent of "yakun" is an implied pronoun, which is the subject of "kun" (be): that is, at the time He says to a thing "Be!", it is. ﴿On the day when the Trumpet is blown﴾ is an adverbial complement (zarf) to His saying ﴿And His is the dominion﴾, like His saying ﴿Whose is the dominion today?﴾ [Ghafir: 16]. It has been said regarding the grammatical analysis (iʿrab) of the verse other than this, but it is weak or eternal (i.e., unfounded). ﴿Knower of the unseen and the seen﴾ is the predicate of an implied subject (khabar mubtada' mudmar).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verses 74–75:

﴿To his father Azar﴾ This is the name of Abraham's father. Its i'rab (grammatical analysis) is either ʿatf bayan (explicative apposition) or badal (substitution). It is not declined (ghayr munsarif) because of foreignness (ʿujmah) and proper nounhood (ʿalamiyyah), not because of a morphological pattern (wazn), since its pattern is that of the active participle (fāʿil), as in ʿAbir and Shalih. It has also been read in the nominative as a vocative (nidaʾ). It has also been said that Azar is the name of an idol, since it is established that the name of Abraham's father was Tarakh. On this view, it is possible that it was a laqab (epithet) applied to him because he was constantly attached to it, or that the intended meaning is "the worshipper of Azar," in which case the modified noun was deleted and the modifier (muḍāf ilayh) was placed in its position; but this is remote. It is not unlikely that he had two names.

﴿We show Abraham the malakut (dominion) of the heavens and the earth﴾ It has been said that God lifted the heavens and the earth for him until he saw with his own eyes the highest and the lowest realms. This requires a sound transmission. It has also been said that he saw what people see of the malakut, but he attained through it such reflection and inference as no one of his time attained.

﴿And so that he may be﴾ This is connected to a deleted element whose estimated meaning is: "And so that he may be among the certain (al-muqinin), We did that with him."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verses 76–79:

﴿When the night covered him﴾, i.e., concealed him. It is said: "The night covered him (janna 'alayhi al-layl) and concealed him (ajannahu)." ﴿He saw a star and said: "This is my lord."﴾ It is possible that what happened to Ibrahim with the star, the moon, and the sun occurred before he reached puberty and was under obligation. It has been narrated that his mother gave birth to him in a cave, out of fear of Namrud, for he used to kill the infants, because the astrologers had informed him that his destruction would come at the hand of a boy. It is also possible that this occurred after he reached puberty and was under obligation, and that he said it to his people in order to refute and rebuke them. This is the more preferred view, because of His saying afterward: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you associate [with Allah]﴾. It is not conceivable that he would say this while alone in the cave, for that would require disputation and refutation of his people. They used to worship idols, the sun, the moon, and the stars, so he wanted to show them the error in their religion and to guide them to the fact that none of these things may rightly be a god, due to the evidence of their having been created. The One who originated them and arranged their rising, setting, and disappearance is the true God alone. His saying "This is my lord" is the speech of one who is fair to his opponent while knowing that he is in error, because that is more effective in leading to the truth and closer to the opponent's return. Then he established the proof against them with his saying: ﴿I do not like those that set﴾, i.e., I do not like to worship things that change, because change is evidence of having been created, and createdness is not an attribute of God. Then he continued on this same method regarding the moon and the sun. When he had made the proof clear and established the argument against them, he openly declared his disavowal of their falsehood, saying: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you associate [with Allah]﴾. Then he announced his worship of Allah and His oneness, saying: ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who created the heavens and the earth﴾, and he described God with a description that necessitates His oneness and His sole possession of dominion. If it is said: Why did he argue with setting rather than rising, when both are evidence of createdness, since both are a transition from one state to another? The answer is that setting is more evident in indicating this, because it is a transition accompanied by vanishing and concealment.

﴿Will you dispute with me concerning God?﴾ That is, concerning faith in God and His oneness. The original form is ﴿أتحاجونني﴾ with two nūns (ataḥājjūnanī), and it has been read with shadda (tashdīd), by assimilating one of them into the other, and with takhfīf (lightening), by deleting one of them. It is disputed whether the first or the second was deleted.

﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him.﴾ Here "mā" means "that which" (alladhī), and he means by it the idols. They had warned him that their idols might strike him with harm, so he said: I do not fear them, because they have no power over anything.

﴿Except that my Lord wills something.﴾ Here ﴿إلا﴾ (illā) is an exceptive particle that is disconnected (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), meaning "but" (lākin): that is, I only fear my Lord, should He will something for me.

﴿And how should I fear what you associate, when you do not fear to associate with God what has no authority from Him?⌝ That is, how should I fear your partners who have no power over anything? And you do not fear what is truly the greatest cause of fear, namely your associating others with God, while you deny me security in a place of security and do not deny yourselves security in a place of fear? Then he confronts them with this by saying: ﴿So which of the two parties is more deserving of security?﴾ meaning the party of the believers and the party of the disbelievers. Then he answers the question with His words: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾ — the verse. It was also said that "those who believe" is a new statement (istiʾnāf) and not part of Abraham's speech.

﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing.﴾ When this verse was revealed, the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) were troubled by it and said: "Which of us has not wronged himself?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "It is only as Luqman said to his son: ﴿O my son, do not associate anything with God; indeed, association is a tremendous wrong﴾" (Qur'an 31:13).

﴿And that was Our argument﴾: a reference to the reasoning and argumentation he had presented earlier.

﴿And among his descendants﴾ (dhurriyyah, offspring or descendants). The pronoun refers to Ibrahim or to Nuh, peace be upon them both. Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 6, verse 90:

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided﴾: a reference to the prophets mentioned earlier. ﴿So follow their guidance﴾. This is cited by those who argue that the law of those before us is law for us. As for the foundations of religion (uṣūl al-dīn), namely tawhid, belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers and the Last Day, all nations and laws agree on them. As for the branches (furū'), the laws differ on them. The disagreement is whether the Prophet (ﷺ) should follow those before him in them or not. The hā' in iqtadih is a pause marker (hā' al-waqf), so it should be dropped when reading continuously, but whoever writes it does so in keeping with its form in the Mushaf.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 91:

﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾, meaning: they did not know Him with true knowledge, in His gentleness toward His servants and His mercy toward them; for they denied that He sent messengers and revealed books. The ones who said this were the Jews, as evidenced by what follows. They said it in exaggeration in denying the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). It is narrated that the one among them who said it was Malik ibn al-Sayf. So God refuted them by holding them to what they cannot but acknowledge, namely the revelation of the Torah to Musa. It was also said: the ones who said it were the Quraysh, and they were held to this because they used to affirm the Torah.

﴿And you were taught what you did not know﴾. The address is to the Jews or to the Quraysh, by way of establishing proof and refuting them in their saying: "God has not revealed anything to a human." If it is to the Jews, then what they were taught is the Torah; if it is to the Quraysh, then what they were taught is what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought.

﴿Say: "God"﴾: this is the answer to "who revealed it?" The word "Allah" is in the nominative case, either governed by an implied verb whose estimated form is "God revealed it," or as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada').

Translation:

﴿And that you may warn﴾ is a conjunction governed by the attribute of the Book. ﴿Umm al-Qura﴾ (the Mother of Cities) is Makkah. It was called Umm al-Qura because it is the place of the first House established for mankind, because it has been reported that the earth was spread out (dahiya) from it, and because the people of the towns come to it on pilgrimage from every deep ravine.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 93:

﴿أَوْ قَالَ أُوْحِيَ إِلَيَّ﴾ ("Or [who] says: 'It has been revealed to me'"): this is Musaylima and others of the liars who claimed prophethood.

﴿وَمَن قَالَ سَأُنزِلُ مِثْلَ مَآ أَنَزلَ ٱللَّهُ﴾ ("And [who] says: 'I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed'"): this is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, because he opposed the Qur'an. The wording is general, encompassing him and others among the mockers.

﴿وَلَوْ تَرَىۤ﴾ ("And if you could see"): its response is omitted; its estimated meaning is: "you would see a tremendous matter." 

﴿وَالظَّالِمُونَ﴾ ("and the wrongdoers"): these are those previously mentioned, namely the Jews, the liars and the mockers, in which case the definite article (al-lam) is for prior reference (al-'ahd). It may also be more general than that, in which case the article is for the category (al-jins).

﴿بَاسِطُوۤاْ أَيْدِيهِمْ﴾ ("stretching out their hands"): i.e., the angels stretch out their hands toward the disbelievers, saying to them: "Bring out your souls." This is an expression of rebuke in the context and of severity in the taking of souls.

﴿ٱلْيَوْمَ تُجْزَوْنَ﴾ ("Today you will be recompensed"): it may mean that very moment itself, or the extended time from then until eternity.

﴿ٱلْهُونِ﴾ ("humiliating"): the abasement.

﴿Furada﴾ means alone, separated from your wealth and children, or from your partners. The first meaning is preferred because of His saying: ﴿and you have left behind what We bestowed upon you﴾, that is, what We gave you of wealth and children. The second meaning is preferred because of His saying: ﴿and We do not see with you your intercessors﴾. ﴿Laqad taqatta'a baynakum﴾ means your union has been scattered. Whoever reads "تَّقَطَّعَ" with a nominative ending (raf') attributes the verb to the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) and uses it as a noun. In that case "البين" means separation, or it may mean connection. Whoever reads it with an accusative ending (nasb) takes the subject to be the verbal noun (masdar) of the verb, or the subject is omitted, its estimate being "تقطع الاتصال بينكم", meaning the connection between you has been cut.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 95:

﴿Indeed, He is the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾ i.e., He splits the grain beneath the earth for the emergence of plants from it, and He splits the date-stone for the emergence of the tree from it. It has been said: He meant the two splits that are in the date-stone and the wheat-grain, and the first (view) is more preferred because of its generality over the varieties of grains. ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead﴾ this was mentioned in Al ʿImran. ﴿And the Brings forth the dead from the living﴾ is conjoined to "Splitter."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 96:

﴿Fāliq al-Iṣbāḥ﴾ (the Cleaver of the Dawn), meaning al-Ṣubḥ (the dawn). It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that has been used as a name for the dawn. The meaning of its cleaving (falq) is that He brings it out from the darknesses. It has also been said: the darkness is what splits open to give the dawn, so the sense is "Cleaver of the darkness of the dawn." ﴿Sakanan﴾ (a means of rest), meaning one rests in it from movements and finds repose. ﴿Ḥusbānan﴾ (a means of reckoning), meaning by them the reckoning of times, the night and the day, is known. ﴿Dhālika taqdīru al-ʿAzīzi al-ʿAlīm﴾ (That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing). How excellent is the mention of these two Names here, for al-ʿAzīz (the Almighty) overturns and subdues everything, and He has subdued the sun and the moon and subjected them as He wills. And al-ʿAlīm (the All-Knowing) is for what there is in the decree of the sun, the moon, the night and the day of knowledge, great wisdom, and perfection of craftsmanship.

﴿In the darknesses of the land and the sea﴾: that is, in the darknesses of the night, on land and at sea. He attributed the darkness to them because it envelops them, or he likened the confusing routes to darknesses.

Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 98:

﴿So there is a settled place and a place of temporary deposit﴾. Whoever reads "mustaqarr" with a kasra on the qaf, it is an active participle (ism fa'il), and "mustawda'" is a passive participle (ism maf'ul), and the implied meaning is: among you there is one who is settled and one who is deposited. Whoever reads it with a fatha on the qaf, it is a noun of place or a verbal noun (masdar), and "mustawda'" is likewise, and the implied meaning according to this reading is: for you there is a settled place and a place of temporary deposit. The settling is in the womb (al-Rahmān), and the depositing is in the loins (al-sulb). It was also said: the settling is above the earth, and the depositing is beneath it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 99:

﴿فَأَخْرَجْنَا بِهِ﴾ The pronoun refers to the water. ﴿فَأَخْرَجْنَا مِنْهُ﴾ The pronoun refers to the vegetation (al-nabat). ﴿خَضِراً﴾ means green and tender (akhdar ghaddan), and it comes forth from the base of the plant from its shoots (al-farakh). ﴿نُّخْرِجُ مِنْهُ﴾ The pronoun refers to the greenery (al-khadir). ﴿حَبّاً مُّتَرَاكِباً﴾ means the ear of grain (al-sunbul), because its grains lie upon one another; and likewise the pomegranate and the like. ﴿قِنْوَانٌ﴾ is the plural of qinw, which is a cluster (ʿunqud) of dates. It is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "from the palm trees" (min al-nakhl), and "from its spathes" (min talʿiha) is a substitution (badal). The ṭalʿ (spathe) is the first thing that emerges from the date palm, enclosed in its sheaths (akmam). ﴿دَانِيَةٌ﴾ means near and easy to reach; and it has been said: near to one another. ﴿وَجَنَّٰتٍ مِّنْ أَعْنَٰبٍ﴾ is in the accusative, coordinated with "vegetation of every thing" (nabat kull shay'); it was read in other than the seven canonical readings in the nominative, coordinated with "qinwan". ﴿مُشْتَبِهاً وَغَيْرَ مُتَشَٰبِهٍ﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the olives and the pomegranates, or of everything mentioned previously of the vegetation. "Mushtabih" and "mutashabih" have one meaning: among vegetation is that which resembles one another in colour, taste and form, and among it is that which does not resemble one another. In this there is a decisive proof of the Creator, the Chooser, the All-Powerful, the All-Knowing, the Willing. ﴿ٱنْظُرُوۤاْ إِلِىٰ ثَمَرِهِ إِذَآ أَثْمَرَ وَيَنْعِهِ﴾ means: look at its fruit when it first emerges, weak and without benefit, then it passes from state to state until it ripens (yaynaʿ), that is, matures and becomes sweet.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 100:

﴿شُرَكَآءَ ٱلْجِنَّ﴾ [They made the jinn partners]. The word الجنّ (al-jinn) is in the accusative (naṣb) as the first object (mafʿūl awwal) of جعلوا (ja'alū, "they made"), and شركاء (shurakā', "partners") is the second object (mafʿūl thānī). It was placed first to emphasise the enormity of associating partners with God. Alternatively, شركاء (shurakā') is the first object, and the word لله (lillāh, "for God") occupies the position of the second object, while الجنّ (al-jinn) is an appositive (badal) of شركاء (shurakā'). The intended meaning here is the angels, as a refutation of those who worshipped them. It is also said that the intended meaning is the jinn, and associating them as partners means obeying them.

﴿وَخَلَقَهُمْ﴾ [while He created them]. The و (wa) is for the circumstantial clause (lil-ḥāl), and the meaning is a refutation of them: that is, they made partners for God while He is the one who created them. The pronoun هم (hum, "them") refers either to the jinn or to those who made the partners. The argument stands on both interpretations.

﴿وَخَرَقُواْ لَهُ بَنِينَ وَبَنَٰتٍ﴾ [and they attributed to Him sons and daughters falsely]. That is, they invented and forged. The sons refers to the saying of the Christians about the Messiah and of the Jews about ʿUzayr, and the daughters refers to the saying of the Arabs about the angels.

﴿بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ﴾ [without knowledge]. That is, they said this without any proof or evidence; rather, it is mere fabrication.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verses 101–102:

﴿Badi'** (Originator)﴾ Its meaning was mentioned in al-Baqarah [117]. It is in the nominative either as the predicate of an implied subject, or as the subject whose predicate is: ﴿how can He have a son?﴾ and the agent is God, the Exalted. The purpose of this is to refute those who attributed sons and daughters to God, and this is in two respects. The first: a child can only be of the same kind as its father, and God, the Exalted, is exalted above kinds, since He is their Originator, so it is not valid that He should have a child. The second: God created the heavens and the earth, and whoever is like this is free of need of a child and of everything else. ﴿So worship Him﴾ is a consequence of the content of the sentence, i.e., whoever is like this is the one deserving of worship alone.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 103:

﴿Vision cannot grasp Him﴾, meaning in this world. As for the Hereafter, the truth is that the believers will see their Lord, based on His saying: ﴿Looking at their Lord﴾ [75:23]. There are authentic and explicit hadiths about this which do not admit of interpretation (ta'wil). The Ash'aris said that seeing Allah, exalted is He, in this world is rationally possible (jawaz 'aqlan), because Musa asked it of Allah, and Musa would not ask for something impossible. People have differed over whether the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw his Lord on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey) or not. ﴿And He grasps the vision﴾. Some of them said: the difference between ru'yah (seeing) and idrak (grasping) is that idrak implies encompassing a thing and reaching its extent, so He negated that the eyes of creation grasp their Lord, and that does not entail the negation of seeing. Based on this, the statement ﴿And He grasps the vision﴾ is fitting, due to the encompassing of His knowledge, exalted is He, of hidden things. ﴿He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾, meaning: Subtle beyond being grasped by vision, and He is the All-Aware of everything, and He grasps the vision.

Ibn Juzayy, al-Tashil, on Surah 6, verses 104–106:

﴿قَدْ جَآءَكُمْ بَصَآئِرُ﴾ "Clear proofs have certainly come to you from your Lord." The word is the plural of baṣīra, which is the light of the heart, while baṣar is the light of the eye. This speech is on the tongue of the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿وَمَآ أَنَا عَلَيْكُم بِحَفِيظٍ﴾ "And I am not a guardian over you."

﴿وَلِيَقُولُواْ﴾ "And so that they may say," is connected to an omitted element whose sense is: "they may say, 'You have varied the verses.'"

If it means turning away from fighting them and punishing them, then it is mansūkh (abrogated). Likewise: ﴿وَمَآ أَنَا عَلَيْكُم بِحَفِيظٍ وَلَا وَكِيلٍ﴾ "I am not a guardian over you, nor a trustee."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 6, verses 108–110:

﴿And do not revile those whom they invoke besides God﴾, meaning: do not revile their deities, for that would become a cause for them to revile God. The Malikis (the Maliki school of law) used this verse as evidence for *sadd al-dhara'i'* (blocking the means that lead to a prohibited outcome). ﴿Say: Signs are only with God﴾, meaning: they are in the hand of God, not in my hand. ﴿And what will make you aware﴾, meaning: what will make you know. It derives from *shu'ur* (awareness) of a thing, and *ma* here is either negative or interrogative. ﴿That when they come, they will not believe﴾. Whoever reads *anna* with a fatha, it is the object of *yush'irukum* (will make you aware), meaning: what will make you know that when the signs come to them, they will not believe in them? We know this, and you do not know it. It was also said that *la* is extra, and the meaning is: what will make you aware that they will believe? It was also said that *anna* here means *la'alla* (perhaps). Whoever reads it with a kasra, then it is a resumptive statement, and the speech is complete at His words: "And what will make you aware," meaning: what will make you aware of what will happen from them. Thus, according to the reading with a kasra, one stops at *ma yush'irukum*. As for the reading with a fatha, if *anna* is a verbal noun (*masdariyya*), one does not stop there, because it is governed by the preceding verb. If it means *la'alla*, some scholars permitted stopping there, but our shaykh Abu Ja'far Ibn al-Zubayr prohibited it, because *la'alla* carries the sense of causation. ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sight﴾, meaning: We seal them and prevent them from understanding, so they do not comprehend. ﴿As they did not believe in it the first time﴾. The *kaf* here indicates causation, meaning: We seal their hearts and sight as a punishment for them, because they did not believe in Him the first time. It may also be a *kaf* of comparison, meaning: We seal them when they see the signs, just as We sealed them the first time.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 111:

﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾ etc.: It is a refutation of their oath that, if a sign came to them, they would surely believe in it; i.e., even if We gave them these signs that they proposed, and every sign, they would not believe unless Allah wills. ﴿Qubulan﴾ with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba', i.e., face to face (mu'ayanah), so it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). It is also read with two dammas, and its meaning is confrontation, like His saying ﴿and it was torn from the back, and they met her master at the door﴾ [Yusuf: 26], where qudda min qubul is used. It was also said: it is the plural of qabil in the sense of kafil (guarantor), i.e., guarantors of the truth of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 112:

﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy﴾ etc.: a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ) by way of taking comfort in the example of others. ﴿Devils of mankind and jinn﴾, that is, the rebellious among both kinds. The word shayatin (devils) is in the accusative either as a substitute (badal) for ʿaduwwan (enemy), since it carries the sense of a plural, or as the first object, with ʿaduwwan as the second object. ﴿Some of them inspire to others﴾, that is, they whisper and cast evil. ﴿Embellished speech as deception﴾, meaning the falsely adorned words that they make attractive. ﴿And had your Lord willed, they would not have done it﴾: the pronoun refers either to their inspiration or to the enmity of the disbelievers. ﴿So leave them﴾: a warning (waʿid). ﴿And what they fabricate﴾: "ma" here is in the accusative position, either as an object of accompaniment (maf'ul maʿah) or as a conjunction with the pronoun (ʿatf ʿala al-damir).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 113–115:

﴿وَلِتَصْغَىٰٓ﴾ meaning "so that it may incline," i.e., lean toward it. It is related to a deleted element, and the lam is the lam of result (lam al-sayrura, indicating what eventually comes about). ﴿إِلَيْهِ﴾ The pronoun refers to their inspired whisperings (wahyihim). ﴿وَلِيَقْتَرِفُوا﴾ meaning "that they may earn" or "acquire." ﴿أَفَغَيْرَ ٱللَّهِ﴾ is the object of a deleted verb of saying, meaning: say to them, "Shall I seek a judge other than Allah?" ﴿وَتَمَّتْ كَلِمَتُ رَبِّكَ﴾ meaning "and the word of your Lord has been fulfilled," i.e., it has come true. The "words" (kalimat) are what He sent down to His servants of His books. ﴿صِدْقًا وَعَدْلًا﴾ meaning: truthful in what He reports, and just in what He judges.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verses 118–119:

﴿So eat of what they catch for you, and mention the name of Allah over it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 4]. The purpose of this command is to permit what has had the name of Allah mentioned over it, and to prohibit what is slaughtered for idols (nusub) and other things, as well as carrion (maytah). This prohibition is implied by the implication of the command (dalil al-khitab, the reasoning drawn from what a discourse implies), and it was then stated explicitly in His words that follow: ﴿That you not eat of what has not had the name of Allah mentioned over it﴾. Those who hold that mentioning the name of Allah (tasmiyah) is obligatory on the slaughtered animal have used this verse as evidence. However, the discourse came in the context of prohibiting carrion and other things. If we interpret it in that context, there is no evidence in it for the obligation of mentioning the name over the slaughter of Muslims. But if we interpret it in its general sense, then it is evidence for that. 'Ata' said: this verse is a command to mention the name of Allah at the slaughter, at the eating, and at the drinking. ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not eat﴾: meaning, what reason do you have for refraining from eating of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, when He has already made clear to you the lawful from the unlawful? ﴿Except what you are compelled to﴾: this is an exception from what has been prohibited.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 120–121:

﴿And leave the outward and the inward of sin﴾. The term encompasses all kinds of sins, for all of them are either inward or outward. It has also been said: the outward refers to deeds, and the inward refers to belief. ﴿And indeed, it is grave disobedience﴾. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verses 122–123:

﴿Is he who was dead and We gave him life﴾: Death here is a metaphor for disbelief (kufr), life is a metaphor for faith (iman), and the light is the light of faith, while the darknesses are disbelief. They are metaphors (isti'arat). In His words ﴿dead and We gave him life﴾ there is an antithesis (mutabaqa), which is among the tools of eloquent expression (bayan). The verse was revealed concerning 'Ammar ibn Yasir, and it was said concerning 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. The one in the darknesses is Abu Jahl, but its wording is more general than that. ﴿like one whose likeness is⦆: "mathal" here means "sifa" (attribute), and it was said it is superfluous (za'ida), and the meaning is "like one who is". ﴿And thus We placed in every town its greatest criminals﴾: that is, just as We placed in Makkah its greatest men (akabir) so that they might plot therein, We placed in every town. He mentioned only the greatest because others follow them. The purpose is to console the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿its criminals (mujrimiha)﴾: its grammatical analysis (i'rab) is that it is a genitive construction (mudaf ilayhi) according to al-Farisi and others. Ibn 'Atiyya and others said: the first object of "ja'alna" is "akabir", and the second object is fronted (muqaddam). This is good in meaning but weak in Arabic, because "akabir" is the plural of "akbar", which is of the form "af'al", and such a form is only used with "min" or in a construct (idafa).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 124:

﴿They said: "We will never believe until we are given the like of what the messengers of Allah were given."﴾ The verse: The one who uttered this statement was Abu Jahl, though it is also said it was al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, for he said: "I am more deserving of prophethood than Muhammad." ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message.﴾ This is a rebuttal to them concerning what they demanded. The meaning is that Allah knew that Muhammad (ﷺ) was fit for the message, so He singled him out for it, and He knew that they were not fit for it, so He withheld it from them. In the verse there is one of the devices of rhetoric, the repetition (al-tardid), since He concluded their speech with the name of Allah and then returned to it at the beginning of His own speech. ﴿Humiliation (sagar)⦆ means abasement (dhilla).

﴿He will open his breast to Islam.﴾ Expanding the breast (sharḥ al-ṣadr) and its constriction and tightness (ḍīq and ḥaraj) are borrowed expressions (isti'āra, metaphor). Whoever reads ﴿ḥarajan﴾ with a fatḥah on the rāʾ treats it as a verbal noun (maṣdar, the infinitive used as a noun) functioning as a description. ﴿As if he were climbing up into the sky.﴾ That is, as if he were trying to ascend to the sky, which is impossible. Likewise, faith becomes difficult for him. The underlying form of the doubled ﴿yaṣṣaʿʿadu﴾ is *yataṣaʿʿadu*, and it was also read with the doubling reduced (taxfīf).

﴿Dār al-Salām﴾ (the Abode of Peace): Paradise. Here "al-Salām" may be a name of Allah, and so He attributes the abode to Himself, because it is His possession and His creation. Or it may mean safety and greeting.

﴿And the day He will gather them﴾. The governing element (al-'amil, the word that grammatically governs) of the word "يوم" (yawm, "day") is an omitted verb whose estimated form is "اذكر" (udhkur, "remember"), and its estimated form is "قلنا" (qulna, "We said"). Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 130:

﴿Did there not come to you messengers⁠﴾ is an address (taqrir) to the jinn and mankind. It is said: the jinn were sent messengers from among themselves, based on the apparent meaning of the verse. It is also said: the messengers were from mankind only. He said "messengers from among you" because He included both the two weighty ones (al-thaqalan) in the address. ﴿And they will testify against themselves⁠﴾ — there is no contradiction between this and their saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists⁠﴾, because that was discussed earlier. If it is asked: why did He repeat their testimony against themselves? The answer is that their saying "we testify against ourselves" is a statement they made, whereas His saying "they testified against themselves" is a humiliation for them and a condemnation of their state.

**﴿That﴾** is the predicate of an implied subject, its implied sense being "the matter is that," or it is an object of an implied verb, meaning "We did that." The demonstrative refers to the sending of the Messengers. **﴿That He would not﴾** gives the reason for the sending of the Messengers; it stands in the position of an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*), or it is a substitute (*badal*) for "that." **﴿with injustice﴾**: here there are two interpretations. The first is that God would not have destroyed the towns without sending Messengers to them, so that destroying them would have been an injustice, since He had not warned them. This is like His saying: ﴿And We would never punish until We sent a Messenger﴾ [al-Isra: 15]. The second is that God does not destroy the towns for their wrongdoing when they do wrong without first warning them; on this reading, the one who commits the injustice is the people of the towns, and their heedlessness is the absence of warning. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari both related the two interpretations. The first interpretation is sound according to the school of the Mu'tazila, but it is not valid according to the school of Ahl al-Sunna, because if God destroyed His servants without any sin, He would not, in their view, be an unjust one.

ۚ﴿And for each there are degrees﴾ — ranks (manāzil) in recompense for their deeds, of reward and punishment. ﴿from the offspring of a people﴾ — that is, from the descendants of the people of Noah's ark, or of those before them, back to Adam.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 135–136:

﴿Act according to your station﴾ The command here is one of threat, and "al-makanah" means capability (al-tamakkun). ﴿Then you will come to know﴾ a threat. ﴿Whose will be the final abode﴾ may be understood as "man" being a relative pronoun in the accusative position as the object, or as an interrogative in the nominative position as the subject. ﴿The final outcome of the abode﴾ means the Hereafter or the world, and the former is more preferred, due to His saying: ﴿The final abode, gardens of perpetual residence﴾ [al-Ra'd: 22–23].

﴿And they assign to God a share of what He has created of crops and livestock﴾ The pronoun in "ja'alu" (they assigned) refers to the pagan Arabs. Al-Suhayli said: they are a tribe from Khawlan, known as al-Adim. They used to assign from their crops, fruits and livestock a share for God and a share for their idols. The meaning of "dhara'a" is "created and brought into being," so in this there is a refutation of them, because God, who created and brought them into being, is their owner, and there is no lord besides Him. ﴿By their claim﴾ meaning by their assertion and their saying without evidence or revealed law. "Al-zaʿm" is mostly used for falsehood. It is recited with a fatha on the zay, and al-Kisa'i recited it with a damma, and both are dialectal forms. ﴿So what was for their partners does not reach God﴾ The verse: whenever the wind blew and carried something from what belonged to God to what belonged to the idols, they would let it remain; and if it carried something from what belonged to the idols to what belonged to God, they would return it. And when they were struck by drought, they would eat God's share and withhold their partners' share.
