Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 137:

﴿And thus their associates have made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children﴾ They used to kill their children by burying them alive (al-wa'd) and slaughtering them as offerings (qurban) to the idols. Their "associates" here are: the devils (al-shayatin), or those who attend to the idols (al-qa'imun 'ala al-asnam).

The majority of readers read the zay in zayyana with a fatha, in the active form (al-bina' lil-fa'il), with qatl in the accusative as its object, awladihim in the genitive by annexation (idafa), and shurakauhum in the nominative as the subject of zayyana. The "associates" in this reading are those who made the killing attractive. Ibn 'Abbas read the zay with a damma, in the passive form (al-bina' lil-maf'ul), with qatl in the nominative as the deputy subject (naib al-fa'il), awlad in the accusative as the object of qatl, and shurakã'ihim in the genitive by annexation to qatl, being the annexation of the verbal noun to its agent. He separated the annexed term from what it is annexed to by his saying "awladihim," and this is weak in Arabic, though it has been attested in poetry. The "associates" in this reading are the ones who kill the children.

﴿to bring about their ruin (liyurduhum)﴾ meaning: to destroy them, and it derives from al-radan, which means destruction (al-halak).

﴿They say, "These are livestock and tilth set apart (ḥijr)"﴾. That is, forbidden. It is a verb used in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ūl), like *dhibḥ* (the slaughtered animal), so it applies equally to the masculine and feminine, the singular and the plural. ﴿None may eat of them except whom they wish﴾. That is, none may eat them except whom they wished, namely those who served the idols, and men but not women. ﴿And there are livestock whose backs are forbidden﴾. That is, they may not be ridden, and these are the *sawā'ib* (animals set free and left unridden) and their counterparts. ﴿And there are livestock over which they do not mention the name of God﴾. It was said that its meaning is that they do not perform the Hajj on them, so the name of God is not invoked through the *talbiyah* (the pilgrim's chant). It was also said that the name of God is not mentioned over them when they are slaughtered. ﴿Fabricating against Him﴾. They had divided their livestock into these categories and attributed that to God as a fabrication and a lie. It is in the accusative either as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), or as an object of purpose (maf'ūl li-ajlihi), or as an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkid).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verses 139–140:

﴿And they say: "What is in the wombs of these livestock is exclusively for our males, and forbidden to our females."﴾ The verse: They used to say about the fetuses of the baheera and the saiba: whatever is born of them alive is exclusively for the men, and women may not eat of it; and whatever is born of them dead, men and women share in it. The word khāliṣa is feminine to agree with the sense (the meaning being "fetuses"), and the word muḥarram is masculine, agreeing with the wording of "mā" (what). It is also permissible that the ta' (feminine ending) in khāliṣa is for emphasis (mubālagha). ﴿And they have forbidden what Allah has provided for them﴾, that is, the baheera, the saiba and the like.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verses 141–142:

﴿Gardens, some trellised and some not trellised﴾: "Trellised" means raised up on supports and the like. "Not trellised" means left spreading upon the face of the earth. It is also said: the trellised ones are those that people planted in inhabited areas, and the untrellised ones are those that God caused to grow in the mountains and the wilderness. ﴿Diverse in its produce﴾: in colour, taste, smell and size. This is evidence that the Creator is one who chooses and wills. ﴿And give its due on the day of its harvest﴾: It is said that its due here is the zakat (obligatory almsgiving). This view is weak for two reasons. The first is that the verse is Meccan, whereas zakat was made obligatory in Medina. The second is that zakat is not given on the day of harvest; it is given on the day the grains and fruits are gathered together. It is also said that its due is what is given in charity to the needy on the day of harvest, and that this was obligatory and then abrogated (naskh) by the tithe (ushr). It is also said that it is what falls from the ears of grain, and the command according to this view is recommended (nadb) rather than obligatory. ﴿Some for carrying and some for flat-lying﴾: this is conjoined to "gardens." The "hamulah" (carrying animals) are the large ones, and the "farsh" (flat-lying animals) are the small ones, such as the calves, plural of ʿijl, and the young camels (fisal). It is also said that the hamulah are camels, because they are carried upon, and the farsh are sheep, because they are laid down for slaughter and what is woven from their wool is spread out.

﴿Eight pairs﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "carrying animals and those for spreading (on the ground)." Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 145–146:

﴿Say, "I do not find﴾ the verse requires that the prohibited things be limited to what is mentioned. The Sunnah, however, has prohibited things not mentioned here, such as the flesh of domestic donkeys. So some people held that the Sunnah abrogated (naskh) this limitation. Others held that the verse was revealed on a particular occasion (sabab), and therefore does not imply limitation. Still others held that whatever is other than what is mentioned was forbidden only as a matter of disapproval (karahah), not as a matter of prohibition (tahrim). ﴿Or a sin﴾ is conjoined to the accusatives before it, and it refers to that over which something has been invoked other than the name of God. He called it a sin (fisq) because it immerses deeply in sin. The discussion of these prohibited things has already been given in Surat al-Baqarah [173]. ﴿Every animal with claws﴾ means that which has a digit from among beasts and birds, as stated by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Atiyyah said: it is intended to refer to camels, geese, ostriches and the like, from among animals whose toes are not separated, or which have a hoof. al-Mawardi said the same. al-Naqqash related from Tha'lab that everything that does not hunt is clawed (dhu zufr), and what hunts is dhu makhlab (having talons). This is not consistent, because the lion is dhu zufr. ﴿Except what their backs carry﴾ means the fat on the backs and flanks. ﴿Or the entrails﴾ (al-hawaya) are the intestines (al-maba'ir). It was said: the viscera, the bowels and similar things that are enclosed within the belly. The singular of hawaya is hawiyah, on the pattern of fa'ilah, so the pattern of hawaya on this view is fa'a'il, like sahifah and sahaif. It was said: its singular is hawiyah on the pattern of fa'ilah, so hawaya on this view is fawa'il, like daribah and dawarib. It is conjoined to what is in His saying "except what their backs carry," so it is among what is excepted from the prohibition. It was said: it is conjoined to the backs, so the meaning is "except what the backs carry, or what the entrails carry." It was said: it is conjoined to the fats, so it is among what is forbidden. ﴿Or what is mixed with bone﴾ means what is in the whole body. ﴿And indeed We are truthful﴾, that is, in what We have informed you of concerning the prohibition, and in this is an implicit rebuke of those who prohibited what God did not prohibit.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 147:

﴿And if they deny you, say: "Your Lord is the possessor of vast mercy."﴾ That is, if they deny you regarding what you have informed them of concerning the prohibitions, then say to them: "Your Lord is the possessor of vast mercy," since He does not hasten to punish you despite the severity of your crime. This is like when you say upon seeing a sin: "How forbearing God is!", meaning for His delaying [punishment] from the like of that. Then He followed the description of Him as vastly merciful with His saying: ﴿And His punishment is not turned back from the criminal people.﴾ That is, do not be deceived by the vastness of His mercy, for His punishment is not turned back from the likes of you, either in this world or in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verses 148–150:

﴿Those who associated partners with Allah will say: "If Allah had willed, we would not have associated [anything with Him], nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything."﴾ The meaning of the verse is that they say: their polytheism and their prohibitions of what they forbade occurred by the will of Allah, and if Allah had willed that they not do that, they would not have done it. Thus they argued for this by Allah's will, and that is a fatalistic (jabriyyah) impulse. There is no proof for them in this, because they are obligated and commanded not to associate anything with Allah, not to make lawful what Allah has forbidden, and not to forbid what Allah has made lawful. Will (irada) is distinct from obligation (taklif). It is possible in my view that their saying ﴿If Allah had willed﴾ is something they will say in the Hereafter, in the manner of wishing that it had not occurred, like your saying when you regret something: "If Allah had willed, this would not have happened." That is, they wish that it had not occurred. This is supported by the fact that He related their saying with the future particle, which is the sin (sa), and that is evidence that they will say it in the future, which is the Hereafter.

﴿Say: "Do you have any knowledge that you can produce for us?"﴾ This is a demand for them to state their evidence and a demonstration of their incapacity.

﴿Say: "To Allah belongs the conclusive argument."﴾ When He refuted their argument, He established the argument of Allah, so that the truth may become manifest and falsehood be nullified.

﴿Halumma (bring forth)﴾: it is said that it means "hat" (bring), in which case it is transitive; and it is said that it means "aqbil" (come forward), in which case it is intransitive. According to some Arabs it is a verb to which the pronoun of the dual, the plural and the feminine attach; according to others it is a verb-noun (ism fi'l), addressed in the same way to the singular, the dual, the plural and the feminine. The purpose of the verse is to show their incapacity to produce witnesses.

﴿If they bear witness, then do not bear witness with them﴾, i.e., if they lie in their testimony and fabricate it, then do not testify with the like of their testimony.

﴿Say: "Do you have any knowledge that you can produce for us?"﴾ This is a demand for them to state their evidence and a demonstration of their incapacity.

﴿Say: "To Allah belongs the conclusive argument."﴾ When He refuted their argument, He established the argument of Allah, so that the truth may become manifest and falsehood be nullified.

﴿Halumma (bring forth)﴾: it is said that it means "hat" (bring), in which case it is transitive; and it is said that it means "aqbil" (come forward), in which case it is intransitive. According to some Arabs it is a verb to which the pronoun of the dual, the plural and the feminine attach; according to others it is a verb-noun (ism fi'l), addressed in the same way to the singular, the dual, the plural and the feminine. The purpose of the verse is to show their incapacity to produce witnesses.

﴿If they bear witness, then do not bear witness with them﴾, i.e., if they lie in their testimony and fabricate it, then do not testify with the like of their testimony.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verses 148–150:

﴿Those who associated partners with Allah will say: "If Allah had willed, we would not have associated [anything with Him], nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything."﴾ The meaning of the verse is that they say: their polytheism and their prohibitions of what they forbade occurred by the will of Allah, and if Allah had willed that they not do that, they would not have done it. Thus they argued for this by Allah's will, and that is a fatalistic (jabriyyah) impulse. There is no proof for them in this, because they are obligated and commanded not to associate anything with Allah, not to make lawful what Allah has forbidden, and not to forbid what Allah has made lawful. Will (irada) is distinct from obligation (taklif). It is possible in my view that their saying ﴿If Allah had willed﴾ is something they will say in the Hereafter, in the manner of wishing that it had not occurred, like your saying when you regret something: "If Allah had willed, this would not have happened." That is, they wish that it had not occurred. This is supported by the fact that He related their saying with the future particle, which is the sin (sa), and that is evidence that they will say it in the future, which is the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 151:

﴿Say: "Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you."﴾ God commanded His Prophet ﷺ to call all of creation to listen to the recitation of what has been forbidden to them. In these verses He mentioned the prohibitions upon which all the revealed laws (shara'i') agree, and which were never abrogated (naskh) in any religious community (milla). Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the words that God revealed to Musa (Moses).

﴿That you associate nothing with Him.﴾ It has been said: "an" (أن) here is a particle of explanation and interpretation (harf 'ibara wa-tafsir), so it has no place in i'rab (the grammatical analysis of case endings), and "la" is a prohibitive particle that jazama (apocopated) the verb. It has also been said: "an" is a verbal-source particle (masdariyya) in the nominative position, its implied sense being: "the command is that you not associate", so "la" in this case is a negative particle. It has further been said: "an" is in the accusative position as a substitute (badal) for the phrase "what your Lord has forbidden." This is only valid if "la" is a supplementary (za'ida) particle; if it is not supplementary, the meaning is corrupted, because what was forbidden would then be the abandoning of associating partners. In my view, the better opinion is that "an" is a verbal-source particle in the accusative position as a substitute, and "la" is a negative particle, and the corruption of meaning mentioned does not follow, because his saying "what your Lord has forbidden" means "what your Lord has enjoined upon you," as shown by his saying at the end of the verse.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 152:

﴿That is what He has enjoined upon you﴾ "Bihi" (by it). The word "tahrim" (prohibition) has therefore been taken to carry the meaning of "wasiyya" (enjoining, charge). The meaning of "wasiyya" is more general than that of "tahrim," because an enjoining may be a prohibition or a permission, an obligation or a recommendation. There is no objection to his intending by "tahrim" the wider sense, since the Arabs sometimes mention a specific term and intend by it generality, just as they mention a general term and intend by it specificity. Once this is established, the sense of the statement is: "Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has enjoined upon you," and then it is replaced by an explanatory clarification of it, so he said: ﴿that you associate nothing with Him﴾, meaning: He enjoined upon you that you not associate anything with Him, and enjoined upon you kindness to parents, and enjoined upon you that you not kill your children. Thus the "wasiyya" comprises abandoning association, doing kindness to parents, and what follows after that.

This interpretation which we have adopted is supported by the fact that the verses contain commands, such as kindness to parents, speaking justly, and fulfilling the measure and weight, and prohibitions, such as association, killing a soul, and consuming the property of orphans. Therefore the term placed at the beginning must be a term that comprises both commands and prohibitions, since they are summarized in it and then explained afterwards. The term "wasiyya" is suitable for this, because it comprises both the command and the prohibition. For this reason we have made "tahrim" carry the meaning of "wasiyya," and the mention of the term "wasiyya" afterwards confirms this. If it is not interpreted as we have stated, the verse would present a difficulty, namely the coordination of commands with prohibitions and of prohibitions with commands, for commands demand the performance of an act and prohibitions demand its abandonment, while the conjunctive particle "waw" requires the joining of the conjoined and the conjoined-to, and this is only valid in the manner we have interpreted, namely the generality of the "wasiyya" to both doing and abandoning.

In my view the verse may bear another interpretation, namely that the term "tahrim" is to be taken in its literal sense and includes the doing of prohibited acts and the abandoning of obligatory acts, because abandoning obligatory acts is forbidden. ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isra: 31]. "Imlaq" means poverty, and "min" here is causal; its estimated sense is: "because of poverty." He forbade killing children only because of poverty, since the Arabs used to do this, so the statement came out in the form of what was usual, and it is not understood from it that killing them is permitted for any other reason. ﴿What is apparent of them and what is hidden﴾ [al-An'am: 151]. It has been said: what is apparent is fornication, and what is hidden is taking paramours; but the correct view is that this is general to all indecencies. ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾ [al-Isra: 33]. This is explained by the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except in one of three cases: adultery after marriage, apostasy after faith, or killing a soul without a soul [in retaliation]."

﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan, except in the best manner﴾. The prohibition of approaching comprises all modes of disposal, and in it is the blocking of means (sadd al-dhara'i') (a legal principle of closing avenues that lead to what is forbidden), for when he forbade approaching the property, the forbidding of consuming it is more fitting and more worthy. "The best manner" means the benefit of the orphan and the growth of his wealth. ﴿Until he reaches his maturity (ashuddahu)﴾: this is maturity together with sound judgment (rushd), and the intended meaning here is not age alone, but his knowledge of his own interests. ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾. When He commanded justice in measuring and weighing, and it was known that the exact justice in which there is neither excess nor deficiency is something in which hardship falls and whose attainment is not certain, He commanded what is within capacity of that and pardoned what is other than it. ﴿And even if it be a near relative﴾: that is, even if the one spoken to or against in testimony or otherwise is a relative of the speaker, one should not add or subtract, but must be just.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 153:

﴿And that this is My path, straight﴾ The reference of "this" (hadha) is either to the injunctions mentioned earlier or to the whole Sharia. "Wa-anna" (and that) with the hamza opened and with tashdid is coordinated with what came before, or is a direct object of purpose: that is, follow it because "this is My path, straight." It is also read with the kasra, as a new sentence (isti'naf), and with the fatha and takhfif (lightening), as a coordination; in this case it is a lightened form of the heavy (thaqila) particle. ﴿And do not follow the paths﴾ meaning the various roads in religion, such as Judaism, Christianity and other false religions. It also includes innovations (bid'a) and misleading desires (ahwa') as well. In a hadith: "The Prophet (ﷺ) drew a line and then said, 'This is the way of God.' Then he drew lines to his right and to his left and said, 'These are all paths; on each path there is a devil calling to it.'" ﴿So that you are scattered away from His way﴾ meaning, your scattering away from the way of God. The verb is in the imperfect with the taa' of the present tense dropped, and for this reason Abu al-Hasan Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Bazzi read it with tashdid (doubling).

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 6, verse 154:

﴿ثُمَّ آتَيْنَا﴾ is coordinated with (ma'tuf 'ala) "wassakum bihi" (﴿He has enjoined you with this﴾). If it is objected: the giving of the Book to Musa (Moses) preceded this injunction, so how does He join it to it with "thumma" (then)? The answer is that this injunction is ancient for every nation, upon the tongue of its prophet, so the sequence is valid. It has also been said that "thumma" here indicates the order of reports and speech, not the order of time. ﴿Completion [of Our favor] upon the one who did good﴾. In this there are three interpretations.

The first: the meaning is "a completion of the blessing upon the one who did good," meaning from the people of Musa, so the subject of "ahsan" (did good) is a pronoun referring to "alladhi" (the one who), and "alladhi ahsan" is intended to denote the category of the doers of good.

The second: the meaning is "a completion," that is, a bounty or a reward, for what Musa, peace be upon him, did well of obedience to his Lord and conveying His message. According to this, the subject is a pronoun referring to Musa, peace be upon him, and "alladhi" is an attribute of Musa's deed.

The third: "tamaman" means "perfecting," in return for what God has done well to His servants. According to this, the agent is a pronoun referring to God, exalted is He.

Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verses 156–157:

﴿Lest you should say﴾ is in the position of an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi); its estimated sense is: out of aversion that you should say ﴿"The Scripture was revealed only to two groups"﴾ [i.e., the People of the Torah and the People of the Gospel] ﴿"And we were indeed unaware of their study"﴾ meaning: we did not study the like of their study, and we did not know what they studied of the books, so there is no proof against us. Here "an" (that) is a lightened form of the heavy "inna" (indeed). ﴿"Then there has certainly come to you a clear proof"﴾ as an establishment of proof against them. ﴿"And turned away"﴾ meaning: he averted (aʿrada).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 158:

﴿Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them, or your Lord should come, or some of the signs of your Lord should come?﴾ The similar phrase has already been discussed in al-Baqarah [210]. ﴿Some of the signs of your Lord﴾ are the portents of the Hour, such as the rising of the sun from its west. At that point, the faith of an unbeliever will not be accepted, nor the repentance of a sinner. So His words, ﴿no soul will benefit from its faith﴾, mean that the faith of the unbeliever will not benefit him at that time. And His words, ﴿or has not earned good through its faith﴾, mean that whoever was a believer but did not accumulate good deeds before those signs appeared, and then repented once they had appeared, will not benefit, because the door of repentance is closed at that time. ﴿Say: "Wait, [we too are waiting]"﴾ is a warning (wa'id).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 159:

﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion﴾ are the Jews and the Christians. It was also said they are the people of desires (ahl al-ahwa') and innovations (ahl al-bid'a). In a hadith, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Jews split into seventy-one sects, the Christians split into seventy-two sects, and my community will split into seventy-three sects, all of them in the Fire except one." It was asked: "O Messenger of Allah, who is that one?" He said: "Those who are upon what I and my companions are upon." It is also read as fāraqū (فارقوا), meaning they abandoned it. ﴿And they became sects﴾: shiya' is the plural of shi'a, meaning separated groups, each sect following its own school (yatashayyaʿu limadhhabihā). ﴿You have nothing to do with them in anything﴾ means you are free of them (anta barī' minhum).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 160–161:

﴿عَشْرُ أَمْثَالِهَا﴾ ("ten times its like") indicates a great bounty, general to all good deeds and to all who perform them; and it is the least multiplication of good deeds, for it may reach seven hundred and more.

﴿دِيناً قِيَماً﴾ ("a religion, upright") is a substitution (badal) from the position of ﴿إِلَى صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ ("to a straight path"), because its origin is "He guided me to a path," as evidenced by ﴿اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ﴾ ("Guide us to the path"). Qayyim (قَيِّم) is on the pattern fayyil from qiyam (standing), and it is more emphatic than qa'im (قَائِم). It has also been read as qiyaman, with a kasra on the qaf and a light ya, and with a fatha on the ya; and on this reading it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as a description.

﴿مِّلَّةَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ﴾ ("the religion of Abraham") is a substitution (badal) from dinan, or an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 164:

﴿Say: "Shall I seek a lord other than Allah, when He is the Lord of all things?"﴾ This is a rebuke and reproach directed at the disbelievers. The occasion of its revelation was that they invited him (ﷺ) to worship their gods. ﴿He is the Lord of all things﴾ is a proof of Tawhid (the oneness of Allah) and of the negation of lordship from anyone other than Allah. ﴿And no soul earns [sin] except against itself﴾ is a reply to the disbelievers, because they said to him: "Worship our gods, and we will take upon ourselves for you every consequence you fear in your worldly life and in the Hereafter." So this verse was revealed: that is, it is not as you say; rather, the earning of each soul falls only upon itself. ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾: no one shall carry the sins of another. The original meaning of "wizr" is weight, and then it came to be used for sins.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 6, verse 165:

﴿Khalā'if﴾ is the plural of khalifah: that is, some of you succeed others in dwelling on the earth, or "successors" of God on His earth. According to this, the address is to all people. It has also been said that it is addressed to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), because they succeeded the earlier nations. ﴿And He raised some of you above others﴾ is general, covering wealth, rank, strength, knowledge, and everything else in which people are distinguished from one another. ﴿That He may test you in what He has given you﴾: to test your gratitude for what He has bestowed upon you, and your deeds in what He has empowered you over. ﴿Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed He is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.﴾ He combines warning with hope. As for the swiftness of His punishment, it may refer either to this world, for those whose seizure He hastens, or to the Hereafter, because "everything that is to come is near." We ask Allah to forgive us and have mercy on us by His grace and His mercy.
